sections.markdown:
## C — Lane travel part one: keeping right, speed limits and the basic rule, pavement markings, following distance and the space cushion
Knowledge domain: where to drive, Oregon's statutory speeds and the basic rule, what yellow, white and red markings allow, and the space to keep around the car.

FACT_ID: sec03-F01 | anchor: A01
Keep right except when passing a same-direction vehicle, going left of center around an obstruction, on a one-way road, using the center passing lane of a three-lane road, or when traffic personnel direct you. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec03-F02 | anchor: A01
On a two-way road with no center line, each driver must leave at least half the road to oncoming traffic. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec03-F03 | anchor: A01
Whenever you drive left of the center line, for any reason, you must yield to oncoming traffic. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec03-F04 | anchor: A01
To yield means to slow or stop so another vehicle or a pedestrian can continue safely. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec03-F05 | anchor: A01
Leaving an alley, driveway or parking lot without signs or signals, stop before the road and yield to approaching vehicles and pedestrians. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec03-F06 | anchor: A01
Change lanes only when safe, and avoid frequent lane changes. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec03-F07 | anchor: A02
Oregon's maximum limits apply on top of the basic rule, mark the top safe speed in ideal conditions, and hold whether or not posted unless another speed is posted. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec03-F08 | anchor: A02
The statutory limit is 15 mph in alleys and narrow residential areas. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec03-F09 | anchor: A02
The statutory limit is 20 mph in any business district and in a school speed zone. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec03-F10 | anchor: A02
The statutory limit is 25 mph in residential districts, public parks and on ocean shores where vehicles are allowed. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec03-F11 | anchor: A02
Roads fitting no other category are 55 mph unless posted otherwise, and interstate limits vary. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec03-F12 | anchor: A03
Some Oregon speed signs are digital and use road, weather, traffic and visibility sensors to lower the speed when needed, sometimes showing why. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0028]

FACT_ID: sec03-F13 | anchor: A03
Yellow variable advisory speed signs recommend a speed and switch on only when needed; they are not limits, but police may enforce them through the basic rule. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0028]

FACT_ID: sec03-F14 | anchor: A03
Black-and-white variable speed limit signs change the actual limit with conditions and are enforced like any speed limit sign. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0028]

FACT_ID: sec03-F15 | anchor: A03
Lower variable speeds add reaction time when fog, rain or snow cut visibility, and add stopping room on sharp curves, steep hills and construction zones. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0028]

FACT_ID: sec03-F16 | anchor: A03
The basic rule requires a speed that is reasonable and cautious for existing conditions, on every road at all times. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0028]

FACT_ID: sec03-F17 | anchor: A04
Obeying the basic rule means weighing traffic, pedestrians, cyclists, road surface and width, intersection hazards, weather and visibility; it never permits exceeding the limit. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec03-F18 | anchor: A04
A speed unsafe for conditions breaks the basic rule even when it is below the posted limit. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec03-F19 | anchor: A04
If slower than normal traffic, use the right lane or hug the right edge unless preparing to turn left, and pull off at the first safe spot to let a line of traffic pass. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec03-F20 | anchor: A04
Racing is illegal on any road and includes any acceleration or speed contest or a speed record attempt. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec03-F21 | anchor: A04
A federal chart shows a pedestrian hit at 23 mph has a 10 percent risk of death, rising to 50 percent at 42 mph and 90 percent at 58 mph. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec03-F22 | anchor: A05
Oregon pavement markings follow national standards and must be obeyed unless a police officer or road worker redirects you. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec03-F23 | anchor: A05
Yellow lines separate opposing traffic and also edge the left side of one-way roads, ramps, shared left-turn lanes and painted medians; a solid yellow line is the left boundary of one-way roads and ramps. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec03-F24 | anchor: A05
A broken yellow center line marks a two-way road where drivers in both directions may pass. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec03-F25 | anchor: A05
With a solid and a broken yellow line together, you may pass when the broken line is on your side but not when the solid line is. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec03-F26 | anchor: A05
Double solid yellow lines ban passing both ways, but you may turn left across them into or out of a roadway once oncoming traffic clears. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec03-F27 | anchor: A06
Where a two-way left-turn lane exists, turn left only from it; driving along it is illegal, so enter just before the turn and wait there until clear. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec03-F28 | anchor: A06
A painted median edged by double solid yellow lines may be crossed to turn left after oncoming traffic clears, but it is not a turn lane and may not be driven in. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec03-F29 | anchor: A06
Yellow diagonal stripes in a painted median warn of fixed objects or no-vehicle areas, and driving in or turning across them is illegal. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec03-F30 | anchor: A06
White markings divide same-direction lanes, mark the right edge, and form crosswalks, stop lines, symbols and words; a solid white edge or fog line helps you stay on the road. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec03-F31 | anchor: A07
A wide solid white line channels traffic into lanes such as turn lanes and separates bike lanes; crossing it is allowed but discouraged. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec03-F32 | anchor: A07
A broken white line separates same-direction lanes and may be crossed with caution. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec03-F33 | anchor: A07
A dotted white line may be crossed with caution; before an exit or intersection it means your lane leaves the route, at a freeway entrance it means merge, and in an intersection it guides your lane. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec03-F34 | anchor: A07
A double solid white line means no lane changes and usually comes with a sign banning lane changes for a set distance. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec03-F35 | anchor: A07
A marked crosswalk is shown with white lines, and you must stop when a pedestrian is in it. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec03-F36 | anchor: A08
A stop line is a solid white line across your lane where you must stop, and a yield line is a row of triangles pointing at you where you must yield. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec03-F37 | anchor: A08
A bike lane has a wide white line plus a bicycle symbol or bike lane sign and may be painted green. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec03-F38 | anchor: A08
White pavement chevrons may warn of fixed objects ahead or areas closed to vehicles. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec03-F39 | anchor: A08
Red markings show where only transit such as buses, light rail or bikes may travel continuously, but not every transit-only lane is red, so watch signs and markings. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec03-F40 | anchor: A08
A solid red lane is transit only and may read BUS ONLY, BUS BIKE ONLY or LRT, while striped red lines show where cars may cross in to turn, park or reach a driveway. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec03-F41 | anchor: A09
A space cushion is room ahead, beside and behind you; the faster you go, the less time you have to spot hazards and react, and the longer it takes to stop. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec03-F42 | anchor: A09
A safe following distance is 2 to 4 seconds, and above 30 mph it should be 4 seconds or more. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec03-F43 | anchor: A10
To check your gap, count seconds from when the car ahead passes a fixed mark until you reach it; under two seconds means back off and recount. [A10]
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec03-F44 | anchor: A10
Stopped behind a vehicle, stay back far enough to see its rear tires meet the road, and rebuild a safe gap once traffic moves. [A10]
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec03-F45 | anchor: A10
Add following distance on wet roads, when someone behind wants to pass, behind bikes or motorcycles, behind large vehicles that cannot see you, when loaded or towing, and in poor visibility. [A10]
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec03-F46 | anchor: A11
Also add following distance when stopped on a hill, where the car ahead may roll back, while learning to drive, and near or in work zones. [A11]
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec03-F47 | anchor: A11
For side space, avoid riding beside other vehicles on multilane streets, and keep away from oncoming traffic, usually by staying in the center of your lane. [A11]
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec03-F48 | anchor: A11
Make room for vehicles entering a freeway by moving over if the lane is clear, and help signaling drivers by easing your speed slightly. [A11]
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec03-F49 | anchor: A11
Give parked cars extra room within your lane, since a door may open or a person may step out. [A11]
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec03-F50 | anchor: A11
Keep the driver behind you back with a steady speed and an early brake tap that lights your brake lights; if tailgated, move right when there is a right lane. [A11]
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec03-F51 | anchor: A12
If a tailgater stays and you cannot move over, slow gradually to invite a pass, and never brake hard to punish tailgating, since you could be rear-ended. [A12]
Source: [A12 -> pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec03-F52 | anchor: A12
Before backing, look both ways; mirrors miss areas, so turn your head and body right, look out the rear window, glance to each side and back slowly. [A12]
Source: [A12 -> pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec03-F53 | anchor: A12
Stopping distance depends on road and weather, vehicle weight, reaction time and braking, and it grows with speed even in ideal conditions. [A12]
Source: [A12 -> pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec03-F54 | anchor: A12
At 60 mph, the distance from spotting a hazard to a full stop is longer than a football field. [A12]
Source: [A12 -> pdf-0037]

Misconceptions: driving under the limit is not legal if conditions call for slower; an advisory speed is not a limit, yet ignoring it can bring a basic rule citation; a two-way left-turn lane and a painted median are not travel lanes.
Mnemonics: alleys fifteen, business and school twenty, homes and parks twenty-five, otherwise fifty-five; yellow splits opposite directions, white splits the same direction; broken means you may, solid means you may not.
Glossary: basic rule means the duty to drive at a speed reasonable for conditions; space cushion means the open room around your car; fog line means the solid white edge line; yield line means a row of pavement triangles marking where to yield.
Dynamic facts: variable speed signs change the limit or advisory speed with live conditions, and interstate limits vary; obey the sign in front of you.

corpus_stability.reason: The Oregon Driver Manual is a two-year edition (the front cover names a two-year span and the back cover carries a single form revision code); fees and office details are sent to the DMV website rather than printed, and nothing in the selected pages suggests more than one rewrite per year.
